title: Boro: Nvidia's Open-Source Effort for AI-Assisted Linux Kernel Development
content:
Boro: NVIDIA's Open-Source Effort For AI-Assisted Linux Kernel Development
Over the past few months NVIDIA has been developing Boro as a new AI-assisted kernel development CLI written in Rust and focused on local AI for enhancing efficiency for kernel development.
Andrea Righi of NVIDIA has been leading the development of this Boro AI-assisted tooling that is inspired by the successful Sashiko AI tool out of Google and already doing a great job providing code review on the mailing lists. Righi presented on Boro at this week's Linux Plumbers Conference (LPC 2026) in Prague.
Boro is focused on local AI driven patch validation for backporting of patches to older kernels, build/boot/testing of patches, and also plans for detecting possible out-of-tree module breakage. For those without the compute capacity for local AI, Boro also supports using remote OpenAI-compatible servers otherwise there are Claude, OpenCode, and Codex local back-ends.
While Boro is working on its own and can be used by kernel developers today, Righi expressed interest at LPC 2026 in potentially importing some of the functionality into Sashiko itself.
Boro is developed under an Apache 2.0 license. Those wishing to check it out can find Boro via NVIDIA/boro on GitHub. Righi's LPC 2026 presentation can be found at LPC.events.

report.summary: NVIDIA unveiled Boro, an Apache-2.0 Rust CLI that uses local AI to assist Linux kernel patch validation, backporting, and build testing.
report.background: Linux kernel development relies on mailing-list review, manual backporting, and extensive build/boot testing, which can be slow and error-prone. AI-assisted code review has recently gained traction, notably Google's Sashiko, which reviews patches on mailing lists. NVIDIA, a major kernel contributor, has been exploring how local AI can ease maintainer burdens while keeping sensitive code and workflows on developer machines. Boro, led by NVIDIA's Andrea Righi, emerged from that effort and was presented at Linux Plumbers Conference 2026 in Prague. The project reflects a broader trend of AI coding agents moving beyond user-space apps into low-level systems engineering, where reproducibility, privacy, and integration with existing kernel processes matter greatly.
key_points: Boro is an Apache-2.0 licensed CLI written in Rust by NVIDIA, led by Andrea Righi. It draws inspiration from Google's Sashiko AI code-review tool and focuses on local AI to enhance kernel development efficiency. Unlike general coding assistants, it targets the specific workflows of Linux kernel maintainers and developers.

Its initial focus areas include local AI-driven patch validation for backporting patches to older kernel versions, plus building, booting, and testing patches. NVIDIA also plans to add detection of possible out-of-tree module breakage, a common pain point when kernel internals change.

For developers without enough local compute, Boro supports remote OpenAI-compatible servers. It also offers local back-ends such as Claude, OpenCode, and Codex. This flexibility lets users balance privacy, cost, and performance depending on their hardware and security requirements.

Righi presented Boro at Linux Plumbers Conference 2026 in Prague and expressed interest in potentially importing some functionality into Sashiko itself. Boro is already usable by kernel developers today and is available via the NVIDIA/boro GitHub repository; his LPC talk is hosted on LPC.events.
report.impact: For kernel developers, Boro could reduce repetitive review, backporting, and testing work, letting them focus on complex design and debugging. Its local-first design may appeal to maintainers who cannot send proprietary or embargoed code to cloud services. For the AI industry, NVIDIA's entry signals that AI coding agents are expanding from web and app development into low-level infrastructure, where correctness and trust are paramount. It also increases competition with Google's Sashiko and could accelerate standards for AI-assisted kernel workflows. For regular users, faster, more reliable backports and testing may translate into quicker security fixes, better hardware support, and more stable Linux distributions, even if they never interact with Boro directly.
report.tools: Follow NVIDIA/boro on GitHub to try the Apache-2.0 CLI. Compare with Google's Sashiko AI code-review tool. For local back-ends, explore Claude Code, OpenCode, and Codex; OpenAI-compatible servers can be provided by tools like Ollama or LM Studio. Watch Righi's LPC 2026 talk on LPC.events for roadmap details and possible Sashiko integration.
